*Forty years on these fields. I know every patch of this land.*

---

I'm a 59-year-old woman, farming alone since my husband passed. 14 mu is not so much land, but it's plenty for one pair of hands that aren't as young as they used to be. Let me think through what I'll do this season.

**Wheat — 5 mu**
Wheat I always plant in early October, same as my mother did. The tractor man comes to plow — I can't do that myself anymore, costs about 30 yuan per mu but that's fine. I buy the same local variety from the village store that everyone uses. Before planting I spread about half a bag of compound fertilizer per mu — maybe 25 jin spread over the field. In March, when the wheat stands up straight and starts to joint, I go out early morning with a bucket of urea and throw about three or four jin per mu before rain is coming. Water three times: right after planting so the seeds settle, once in spring at jointing, once when the heads are filling out. If spring brings good rain I might skip the third time and save the pumping cost. Machine harvest in early June. I expect maybe 700-800 jin per mu, same as last year.

**Garlic — 2 mu**
Garlic I plant end of September, just before the wheat goes in. I use my own cloves saved from last year's harvest — it saves buying seed but I have to sort them carefully, only the big healthy ones. Garlic takes more fertilizer than wheat. I put down a full bag of compound fertilizer per mu before planting, dig it into the beds. In spring when the green shoots push up I add urea once, and once more in April when I can feel the bulbs swelling underground. Four waterings through autumn and spring. The harvest in late May is the hardest work of my whole year — I have to pull every bulb by hand, tie them, carry them out. I ask my neighbor Liu's son to help me for two days and pay him 80 yuan per day. Garlic price goes up and down but usually sells well.

**Cotton — 3 mu**
My west fields have been cotton for thirty years. I won't give it up even though my daughter keeps saying I should. Plant in late April or early May, after I get the land turned over. One bag of compound fertilizer per mu before planting. During flowering and boll-setting I dissolve some urea in the irrigation water and pump it in. Cotton gets bugs — bollworm especially, also aphids — I spray more times on cotton than any other crop. Water twice in July when it's dry. The picking in September and October is the problem. Three mu is too much for me alone. I hire four people for three days each. I have to — if I wait too long the bolls open and the cotton blows away. I expect maybe 500 jin of seed cotton per mu, around that.

**Chili — 2 mu**
Chili I start from seed inside in early March — fill old basins with dirt and keep them by the south window. Late April I transplant the seedlings to ridged beds. Before transplanting I put compound fertilizer down the middle of each ridge. I fertilize two more times during the season — once when the plants are setting fruit, once in late summer when they're bearing heavily. Chili likes water but the roots rot if it's too wet, so I watch carefully: four waterings but not during rainy periods. I spray for insects and sometimes for a leaf spot disease I get in wet years. Picking goes from August all the way to October, three or four rounds. I need my neighbor's daughter to help for the heavy picking days — she comes three or four days and I pay her. In a normal year, 1,000 jin per mu of fresh red chili.

**Watermelon — 2 mu**
The east plot I do watermelon. I plant in April with black plastic film on the ridges — keeps the soil warm and holds moisture, saves some irrigation. Hybrid seeds from the market: expensive seeds but gives sweet big melons that sell for a good price. I put compound fertilizer in the furrow before laying the plastic. When the melons are setting and swelling I add some urea dissolved in irrigation water. Three waterings total. Watch for cucumber beetles and sometimes white powder on the leaves. Harvest in late June and July. Carrying watermelons is heavy work. I pay Liu's son again to haul them out to the road where the buyer's truck comes. A good year gives maybe 5,000 jin per mu.

**What I worry about**
My biggest worry is labor — not fertilizer, not water. I can do the daily work myself — checking fields, spraying, opening the irrigation valve. But for heavy peak work, I cannot manage alone at my age. I keep back some cash every year for emergencies — if the pump breaks, if I fall sick. So I don't spend everything on inputs. I'd rather do slightly less fertilizer than run out of cash and have nothing for trouble.
